planting.note: Plant in full sun in well-drained, slightly acidic soil; include at least one Honey Bee or comparable pollinizer whenever planting fruiting haskap cultivars.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, slightly acidic soil, and include at least one Honey Bee or comparable pollinizer whenever planting fruiting haskap cultivars, since nearly all commercial haskaps are self-infertile. Honey Bee is a University of Saskatchewan haskap cultivar bred primarily as a universal pollinizer rather than for its own fruit production, chosen for heavy, well-timed flowering that overlaps with most other haskap cultivars' bloom windows. Its berries are edible and pleasantly flavored but smaller and less abundant than dedicated fruiting cultivars like Borealis or Aurora, so it is typically planted as roughly one bush in five or six. The bush is extremely cold-hardy and easy to grow, tolerating the same conditions preferred by other haskaps.

planting.note: Plant rooted cane tips in spring and train onto a wire trellis; cut out fruited canes after harvest and tie in new primocanes for the following season.

Veitchberry is an English hybrid bramble raised in the early twentieth century by the Veitch nursery dynasty, one of several blackberry-raspberry crosses developed in Britain around the same era as the loganberry. It produces large, dark purple-black, conical berries with an aromatic flavor closer to blackberry than raspberry, borne on long, vigorous, thorny trailing canes. It survives mainly in heritage fruit collections and specialist nurseries today, having been largely superseded by more disease-resistant modern hybrids.

planting.note: Grow on a trellis or in a bounded bed in full sun; canes root readily where tips touch soil, so manage spread to keep the planting contained.

directions: Grow on a trellis or in a bounded bed in full sun, and prune out spent floricanes after harvest to keep the stand productive and accessible. Rubus coreanus, known in Korea as bokbunja, is a wild bramble species long harvested and increasingly field-cultivated for its firm, tart berries, most famously fermented into the traditional Korean fruit wine of the same name. The fruit ripens from red to a deep blackish-red, smaller and firmer than typical black raspberries, with a distinctly tart flavor valued in beverages, preserves, and traditional Korean herbal use. Plants form dense, arching, thorny thickets similar to black raspberry and root readily from cane tips that touch the soil, making propagation easy but also requiring management to keep the planting contained.
